question.text: Another new investor subscribes to Kaveri Macro Fund during a DRAWDOWN — the NAV is Rs. 950, but HWM is Rs. 1,000 (the fund is Rs. 50 below HWM). Performance fee is 20%. Under the equalisation mechanism, what happens when the fund subsequently recovers from Rs. 950 back to Rs. 1,000 (a rise of Rs. 50)?

answer.text: The new investor pays 20% performance fee on the Rs. 50 recovery — i.e., Rs. 10 per unit — like existing investors
The new investor is exempt from performance fee until the NAV crosses Rs. 1,050

The new investor receives an equalisation DEBIT (contingent liability) equal to 20% x Rs. 50 = Rs. 10 per unit so that ON RECOVERY TO HWM, the new investor shares the performance-fee payment fairly with existing investors who already experienced the drawdown
The new investor is charged a 5% entry load

explanation.text: **The Logic:** When NAV is BELOW HWM at subscription, the new investor would unfairly benefit from the recovery without paying performance fee — because their personal HWM is lower. To prevent this inequity, an equalisation DEBIT (contingent liability) is booked: on recovery to Rs. 1,000 (existing investors' HWM), the new investor 'owes' 20% x Rs. 50 = Rs. 10 per unit. This keeps fee treatment fair across subscription cohorts. **The Trap:** Option A is wrong because without the debit, the new investor pays on recovery from 950 to 1,000 — but so do existing investors, who are below their HWM. Without equalisation, new investor pays but existing doesn't (drawdown-recovery). Option B overstates the exemption. Option D is fabricated. **Cross-Exam Context:** This is textbook Cat III hedge-fund equalisation mechanics — unique to open-ended daily-NAV funds. Not applicable to Cat I/II. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Book the equalisation debit as a liability on your daily NAV — it reduces the new investor's effective NAV but equalises on HWM recovery. Disclose it explicitly in subscription confirmations to avoid investor disputes.
